title: Stop Telling Grieving People “Everything Happens for a Reason” as Though That Explains the Coffin
paragraphs: Stop Telling Grieving People “Everything Happens for a Reason” as Though That Explains the Coffin
God is sovereign. But that does not mean He appointed you to explain why somebody’s child died, why the cancer came, why the marriage shattered, or why there is an empty chair at the table.
There is a sentence Christians sometimes say because silence frightens us.
We say it at funerals.
We say it in hospital hallways.

We say it while standing beside parents who just buried a child, spouses who just lost the person they expected to grow old with, families still staring at a bedroom nobody has had the courage to clean out.
“Everything happens for a reason.”
And perhaps we mean well.
Perhaps we are desperately trying to defend God.
Perhaps we cannot tolerate watching another human being collapse beneath a question we cannot answer, so we reach into our pocket of Christian phrases and hand them something that sounds theological.
But imagine saying it while the coffin is still in the room.
Imagine a mother touching the polished wood covering the body of the child whose forehead she used to kiss goodnight.
Imagine her hearing:
“Everything happens for a reason.”
What reason?
Tell her.
If you know the particular reason God allowed this particular tragedy, tell her exactly where God revealed it.
If Scripture has not told us, perhaps humility should stop us from pretending heaven whispered an explanation into our ear.
God has reasons.
That does not mean we know them.
And sometimes the holiest thing you can bring into somebody’s suffering is not an explanation.
It is yourself.
That is one of the most haunting lessons hidden inside the opening chapters of Job.
Job’s friends eventually became famous for saying terrible things.
But before their theology became a weapon...
they did something breathtakingly beautiful.
They showed up.
Scripture says Job’s three friends heard about the catastrophe that had fallen upon him and arranged to come to him.
The Hebrew describes their intention:
“לָנֽוּד־ל֖וֹ וּֽלְנַחֲמֽוֹ”
lanud-lo ulenachamo.
They came to sympathize with him, mourn with him, and comfort him.
They did not initially arrive carrying a sermon.
They arrived carrying themselves.
Then they saw Job.
And apparently suffering had altered him so severely that, from a distance, they could hardly recognize their friend.
They wept.
They tore their robes.
They threw dust over their heads.
Then comes one of the most powerful pictures of grief ministry anywhere in Scripture:
“וַיֵּשְׁב֤וּ אִתּוֹ֙ לָאָ֔רֶץ”
Vayeshevu itto la’aretz.
“They sat with him on the ground.”
With him.
Do not miss those two words.
They did not stand over him.
They did not lecture him from a safer emotional altitude.
They came down.
Into the dirt.
Into the silence.
Into the unbearable place where their friend was living.
For seven days and seven nights, they sat there.
Then Scripture says:
“וְאֵין־דֹּבֵ֤ר אֵלָיו֙ דָּבָ֔ר”
ve’ein dover elav davar.
No one spoke a word to him.
Why?
“כִּ֣י רָא֔וּ כִּי־גָדַ֥ל הַכְּאֵ֖ב מְאֹֽד”
Because they saw that his pain—ha-ke’ev—was exceedingly great.
They saw the pain...
and for once, they did not try to conquer it with words.
That may have been the finest ministry Job’s friends ever gave him.
Then they started talking.
And everything changed.
The men who had been compassionate enough to sit beside Job eventually became confident enough to explain Job.
They tried to fit his catastrophe inside their theological equations.
Surely suffering like this must mean something about the sufferer.
Surely Job had done something.
Surely there was a tidy explanation.
But the reader knew something Job’s friends did not.
God Himself had described Job as blameless and upright, a man who feared God and turned away from evil.
The friends were trying to solve a mystery with information they did not possess.
And eventually God Himself confronted them.
Near the end of the book, the LORD tells Eliphaz that His anger burns against him and his two friends because they had not spoken rightly about Him as Job had.
That should sober every Christian who feels compelled to explain another person's suffering.
There is a difference between proclaiming what God has revealed and speculating about what God has concealed.
We can say God is sovereign.
Scripture teaches it.
We can say God is good.
Scripture teaches it.
We can say God can redeem suffering.
Scripture teaches it.
We can say nothing can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
Scripture teaches it.
We can say that for those who love God and are called according to His purpose, God works all things together for good.
Scripture teaches it.
But Romans 8:28 is not permission to invent the hidden reason behind somebody’s funeral.
“All things work together for good” does not mean, “I know why your baby died.”
It does not mean, “Your husband died because God needed another angel.”
Human beings do not become angels when they die.
It does not mean, “God took her because she was too good for this earth.”
Scripture does not tell us that.
It does not mean every tragedy should be followed immediately by an inspirational explanation.
Sometimes faith says, “God knows.”
And humility adds:
“I don't.”
There are mysteries on this side of eternity that Christianity does not require us to pretend we have solved.
The Bible is astonishingly honest about this.
The Psalms contain cries of “Why?”
Habakkuk questioned what he was seeing.
Jeremiah lamented.
Job grieved.
Jesus Himself wept at Lazarus’s tomb.
Think about that.
Jesus knew resurrection was minutes away.
He knew Lazarus would walk out.
He possessed the explanation.
He possessed the power.
He possessed knowledge no mourner standing around that grave possessed.
And still...
“Jesus wept.”
The shortest verse can become one of the longest lessons in pastoral care.
Jesus did not treat tears as theological failure.
He entered them.
And Christianity goes even deeper than saying God watches human suffering from heaven.
The Gospel says God the Son entered our suffering.
Jesus Christ knew betrayal.
Rejection.
False accusation.
Violence.
Humiliation.
Blood.
Nails.
Abandonment.
Death.
The Christian answer to suffering is ultimately not a slogan.
It is a Person with scars.
At Calvary, evil men committed real evil. Jesus truly suffered. The cross was not good because betrayal, torture, injustice, and murder suddenly became good things.
They did not.
Yet God sovereignly accomplished redemption through what wicked hands had done.
That distinction matters.
Christian hope does not require us to call evil good.
It declares that evil cannot defeat God.
The cross looked like the end.
Then came Sunday.
The tomb was sealed.
Then it was empty.
Jesus was dead.
Then the risen Christ walked out.
That is why Christian hope is far stronger than “everything happens for a reason.”
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
Our hope is resurrection.
Our hope is that sin will not have the final word.
Cancer will not have the final word.
The accident will not have the final word.
The cemetery will not have the final word.
Death itself will not have the final word.
Jesus will.
But resurrection hope should never make us cruel about present grief.
You can believe in resurrection while sobbing beside a grave.
You can trust God while asking questions.
You can worship while confused.
You can believe God is sovereign without pretending you understand His secret counsel.
You can tell God, “I don't understand.”
He already knows you don't.
Maybe somebody reading this has been carrying grief while Christians around you kept trying to explain it.
Someone told you to move on.
Someone told you that you should be stronger by now.
Someone quoted a verse before they bothered learning how deeply you were bleeding.
Maybe you started wondering whether something was wrong with your faith because you still cry.
Listen carefully.
Grief is not proof that you have rejected God.
Sometimes grief is the price love pays for having loved deeply in a world where death still tears people apart.
Jesus knew Lazarus would rise.
Jesus still wept.
So cry.
But cry toward Christ.
Ask your questions.
But bring them to Christ.
Fall apart if you must.
But fall toward Christ.
You do not need a complete explanation before you can cling to a complete Savior.
And if you are standing beside somebody who is grieving, resist the pressure to become God's public-relations department.
You do not have to explain everything.
You are allowed to say:
“I don't know why this happened.”
Then stay.
Bring dinner.
Answer the phone.
Remember the anniversary.
Say the dead person's name.
Sit in the uncomfortable silence.
Let them tell the same story for the twentieth time.
Cry when they cry.
Pray when words finally become appropriate.
And when you speak about God, speak only with the confidence Scripture gives you.
Tell them God sees.
Tell them Christ understands suffering.
Tell them Jesus conquered death.
Tell them there is resurrection.
Tell them the Gospel means the grave is not the end for those who are in Christ.
But do not manufacture explanations God has not revealed.
There is something painfully beautiful about Job 2.
The friends saw their friend suffering...
and sat down in the ashes with him.
Maybe somebody in your life needs that version of you.
Not the theologian trying to win an argument.
Not the Christian desperately searching for a sentence impressive enough to make unbearable pain make sense.
Just you.
Present.
Weeping.
Praying.
Listening.
Loving.
Sometimes love sounds like Scripture.
Sometimes love sounds like prayer.
Sometimes love sounds like a meal being placed quietly on the table.

And sometimes love sounds like absolutely nothing because another human being's heart has shattered and you are willing to sit beside the pieces without demanding that they hurry and become a testimony.
If this exposed the way you have spoken to hurting people, don't drown in shame.
Repentance is not the end of the story.
Grace is.
Maybe you once said the wrong thing at a funeral because you didn't know what else to say.
Maybe you quoted something too quickly.
Maybe you tried to explain pain that wasn't yours to explain.
Bring that to Jesus too.
The Gospel is not merely good news for grieving people.
It is good news for people who have wounded grieving people.
At the cross there is forgiveness.
There is mercy.
There is transformation.
There is enough grace to teach us a better way to love.
You do not owe strangers your entire story.
Those three words are enough.
Better yet, send it privately with no demand that they respond.
Save it too.
The day may come when you are standing beside somebody whose world has just collapsed, and you will need to remember that presence can be more faithful than speculation.

And if Gospel Warrior is helping you grow closer to Jesus, consider following and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well. The purpose is not to build an audience around a personality. It is to keep placing Scripture, conviction, Gospel hope, encouragement, repentance, healing, discipleship, and the name of Jesus in front of people who desperately need Him.
It doesn't.
Not because Christians can buy a blessing.
They cannot.
It should not be presented that way.
Give freely, prayerfully, cheerfully, and without coercion.
Send it privately to somebody who needs it.
Pray for the ministry.
Speak the name of Jesus.
The Gospel was never meant to be imprisoned behind a paywall, and the grace of Christ is not merchandise. Our message remains what it has always been:
Jesus saves sinners.
Jesus receives the broken.
Jesus forgives the repentant.
Jesus enters suffering.
Jesus defeats death.
Jesus makes all things new.
And perhaps that is what somebody standing beside a coffin needs most.
Not your theory about why it happened.
Not a polished sentence designed to make tragedy less frightening.
Not an explanation God never gave you.
Maybe they simply need someone willing to sit down in the ashes...
and stay.

Because when every explanation feels too small for the coffin, the wounded do not need us to pretend we know everything God knows—they need us to point, sometimes through tears and sometimes through silence, to the Savior who entered death Himself and came out alive.
The coffin may leave you without an explanation, but because of Jesus, it never gets the final word.
